prompt: A second-order linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients has two distinct characteristic roots. You know its first two terms. What roles do those pieces of information play?

options.text: The roots supply exponential solution patterns; the first two terms determine their weights.
options.explanation: The recurrence fixes the patterns, while initial conditions select one sequence.

options.text: The recurrence coefficients themselves are always the roots.
options.explanation: Roots solve the characteristic equation; coefficients need not equal them.

options.text: One initial term always fixes both weights.
options.explanation: Two independent weights generally require two initial conditions.

options.text: Matching two initial terms makes any formula a solution.
options.explanation: The candidate must also satisfy the recurrence for later terms.

workedExample: First identify patterns that reproduce themselves under the recurrence. Distinct characteristic roots give two independent exponential patterns. Their weighted sum also satisfies the homogeneous recurrence. Then fit both starting values. A formula matching only the initial values can still fail at the next step.

prompt: A genuine second-order linear homogeneous recurrence with constant coefficients has one nonzero characteristic root repeated twice. Why can two weighted copies of the same exponential fail to fit arbitrary starting values?

options.text: Repeated roots mean no sequence exists.
options.explanation: Initial conditions still determine a sequence; the proposed solution family is too small.

options.text: The weights combine into one parameter, so a second independent pattern is needed.
options.explanation: Multiplying the exponential by the index supplies that additional pattern.

options.text: Repeated roots always make the sequence constant.
options.explanation: The root can differ from one, and an index multiplier can also change growth.
They still select the particular sequence.

workedExample: Two copies of exactly the same exponential have the same shape. Adding them only changes one overall weight, leaving too little freedom for two starting values. For a nonzero double root, an index-times-exponential term supplies the second independent solution.
